extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, voters, and policymakers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of The Federalist Papers / New York public)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and justify structural provisions of a written constitution, focusing on appointment mechanisms, executive powers, treaty-making thresholds, and the organization and independence of the judiciary. The guidance assesses which institutional arrangements best secure good administration, stability, and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty ratification proportion (avoid fixed whole-body two-thirds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention 'have gone as far in the endeavor to secure the advantage of numbers in the formation of treaties as could have been reconciled either with the activity of the public councils or with a reasonable regard to the major sense of the community.' It would be impractical to require 'two thirds of the whole number of members' (a fixed proportion of the whole body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer requiring a proportion of the attending members rather than a fixed proportion of the whole body; a fixed required number encourages non-attendance and can amount to near-unanimity, producing impotence, perplexity, and disorder (examples: Roman Tribuneship, Polish Diet, States-General). Requiring a proportion of those present promotes punctuality, keeps the body complete, reduces delays, and better secures the advantages of a numerous agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive co-operation in treaty-making
rubrics_metrics.description: The co-operation of the President in treaty-making provides additional security against improper use of the treaty power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the President co-operates in the treaty process, the people would have greater security under the new Constitution than under the Confederation; the President's involvement is a substantive safeguard in addition to Senate ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of appointing officers — preferred arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment power in ordinary cases ought to be vested either (1) in a single man, or (2) in a select assembly of moderate number, or (3) in a single man with the concurrence of such an assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One man of discernment is better fitted to analyze and estimate peculiar qualities for offices than a body; sole and undivided responsibility begets a livelier sense of duty and regard to reputation, leading to more careful, impartial selection and fewer personal attachments to gratify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination by President with Senate advice-and-consent (check against favoritism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to 'NOMINATE, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint' principal officers; nomination in substance yields the advantages of single-person choice while Senate concurrence provides checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomination lets the President exercise his judgment and bear responsibility as if he appointed; Senate concurrence serves as an 'excellent check' against favoritism, state prejudice, family connection, personal attachment, or pursuit of popularity, and contributes to stability in administration. Senate rejection is unlikely except for strong reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointment power
rubrics_metrics.description: The President 'shall have power to fill up ALL VACANCIES which may happen DURING THE RECESS OF THE SENATE, by granting commissions which shall EXPIRE at the end of their next session.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision allows the Executive to ensure offices are filled during Senate absences, with temporary commissions that expire at the end of the following session—balancing continuity of administration with legislative oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid small private councils of appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere council of appointment (small body) will be a conclave in which cabal and intrigue will have full scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small closed councils (three to five persons) are prone to secrecy, cabal, vote-bargaining, monopoly of employment by a few families, instability if membership rotates, greater susceptibility to executive influence, increased expense, and loss of public responsibility and inspection; therefore they are inferior to the Senate+President arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Representatives unsuitable for appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniting the House of Representatives in the power of making appointments is inappropriate because that body is too fluctuating and too numerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large, frequently changing body (possibly three or four hundred persons in time) would defeat stability of Executive and Senate, cause infinite delays and embarrassments, and thus be unfit for the appointment power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated executive powers (informing, recommending, convening, receiving, executing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The remaining powers of the Executive include giving information to Congress of the state of the Union; recommending measures; convening Congress or either branch on extraordinary occasions; adjourning them when they cannot agree; receiving ambassadors; faithfully executing the laws; and commissioning all officers of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No substantial objections are raised to these powers; they are necessary adjuncts of an energetic Executive and consistent with republican principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial tenure 'during good behavior' (permanency of office)
rubrics_metrics.description: All judges appointed by the United States are to hold their offices 'DURING GOOD BEHAVIOR.' This tenure secures duration in office, provisions for support, and precautions for responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tenure during good behavior is among the most valuable modern improvements: it is a barrier to despotism in a monarchy and to encroachments by the representative body in a republic, and it best secures a steady, upright, and impartial administration of the laws. Permanency is an indispensable ingredient of judicial constitution and 'in a great measure... the citadel of the public justice and the public security.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary's weakness and need for safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary 'has neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment' and is therefore the weakest of the three departments; it must be protected against being overpowered, awed, or influenced by the Executive or Legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the courts lack control of the sword or purse, care (especially permanency in office and institutional separation) is required to enable them to defend themselves and preserve their independence as a bulwark of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power to declare legislative acts void (judicial review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every act of a delegated authority contrary to the tenor of the commission under which it is exercised is void; courts must declare legislative acts void when contrary to the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution is a fundamental law; interpretation of laws is the peculiar province of the courts. Courts are an intermediate body between the people and the legislature to keep the latter within prescribed limits. This does not imply judicial superiority over the legislature but that judges should prefer the superior will of the people (the Constitution) to legislative statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for resolving conflicting laws (last-in-time among equals; prior superior prevails)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two statutes clash, among equals the rule is that 'the last in order of time shall be preferred to the first.' Conversely, between a superior and subordinate authority, the prior act of the superior (i.e., the Constitution) ought to be preferred to the subsequent act of the inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rule of construction adopted by courts to reconcile conflicting laws; it is not derived from positive law. Where a statute contravenes the Constitution, judicial tribunals should adhere to the Constitution and disregard the statute.
